query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor amount of aluminum (e.g., around 5 atomic %) to equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr will form a protective, adherent Al2O3 scale during high‐temperature exposure that improves the alloy’s oxygen resistance while maintaining its useful room- and high-temperature mechanical properties.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy that exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C, but suffers from inadequate oxygen resistance.
generation.intervention: Incorporate approximately 5 atomic % aluminum into the alloy composition.
generation.conditions: Exposure in air at approximately 800 °C for 5 hours with mechanical loads reflective of tensile testing conditions (strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹) and subsequent evaluation of room-temperature and high-temperature performance.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a continuous, thin, and adherent Al2O3 scale on the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: The introduced aluminum, due to its high affinity for oxygen, oxidizes preferentially to form an Al2O3 layer. This oxide scale acts as a barrier to oxygen diffusion into the bulk material, thereby reducing internal oxidation (pesting) without significantly altering the alloy’s mechanical microstructure or compromising its ductility and yield strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Al-doped alloy should exhibit markedly improved oxidation resistance at 800 °C over 5 hours—displaying reduced oxide penetration and pesting—while retaining mechanical properties comparable to the untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.
generation.baseline: The untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy with limited oxygen resistance under high-temperature air exposure.
generation.boundary: Applicable for high-temperature (around 800 °C) air exposure for periods up to 5 hours and under tensile loading conditions (strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹) where preservation of room-temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength is required.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal aluminum concentration is not definitively known; excessive aluminum could lead to the formation of brittle intermetallic phases or negatively impact ductility. Additionally, while the formation of Al2O3 is expected, its long-term adhesion and scale integrity under cyclic conditions remain to be verified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloys: one set of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr and a second set with ~5 atomic % aluminum added. Subject both sets to identical oxidation tests by exposing them to static air at 800 °C for 5 hours. After exposure, perform comprehensive microstructural analysis (e.g., SEM/EDS, XRD) on the surface oxide scales. Assess the mechanical properties using standardized tensile tests at room temperature and high temperature.
measurements: Oxide layer continuity, thickness, and adherence (via SEM, XRD)
Tensile yield strength and ductility measurements at room and elevated temperatures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aluminum-doped alloy does not form a continuous, protective Al2O3 scale (or forms a scale that spalls or is porous) and/or if its tensile properties degrade significantly compared to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Paper card. Question: Can high-entropy alloys be designed to simultaneously achieve high Snoek-type damping capacity, high mechanical strength, and high ductility at elevated temperatures?. System: Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi base HEA, (Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi)98O2 (O-2 HEA), and (Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi)98N2 (N-2 HEA). Processing: Arc-melting of pure metals (purity >99.9 wt%), TiN (99.9 wt%), and TiO2 (99.9 wt%) in a Ti-gettered high-purity argon atmosphere; remelted at least eight times; drop-cast into a water-cooled copper mold (10 mm × 10 mm × 60 mm). Test conditions: Damping measured via multifunction internal friction apparatus at 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, and 4.0 Hz, temperature range 300–1100 K, heating rate 2 K min⁻¹, max strain amplitude 2 × 10⁻⁴; Tensile tests at room temperature, strain rate 1 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹. Findings: The O-2 HEA achieved a peak damping capacity (tanδ_max) of 0.020 at 1.0 Hz, while the N-2 HEA reached 0.027 at 1.0 Hz.; The N-2 HEA exhibited a yield strength of 1362 MPa and elongation of ~11.9%, while the O-2 HEA showed 1138 MPa yield strength and ~20% elongation.; The peak damping temperature (T_p) for the HEAs was approximately 730–747 K at 1.0 Hz, roughly 100 K higher than traditional Snoe
